idiom_name: ordinary object identity (Object#equal?); ActiveRecord == by class and id
implementation_notes: Ruby gives identity semantics by default: Object#equal? is reference equality and the inherited == performs the same comparison, so an ordinary object is already an entity in memory and equal? is the method to reach for once == has been redefined. The identity field is the remaining work - store an immutable id when the object is created - and if the class is backed by ActiveRecord the framework already implements the persistence half: ActiveRecord::Core#== returns true for the same object or for an instance of the same class with an equal id, and hash is derived from class and id, so one row has one comparable identity. When overriding == in a plain class, redefine hash and eql? consistently or Hash and Set membership silently break.
pitfalls: Redefining == to compare attributes changes Hash and Set membership and Array#uniq, because Ruby uses hash and eql? there; if you override ==, override hash and eql? consistently.
ActiveRecord's == returns false for unsaved records and for records fetched without their primary key, even when they denote the same row; do not use it as the only identity check before persistence.
Loading the same row into two ActiveRecord objects yields two ==-equal instances whose attributes can diverge; the identity is shared but the state is not, so edits must be saved in one place.
